topic.title: You're renting the table, not buying coffee
topic.claim: A ₹350 cold coffee is overpriced as a drink and fairly priced as two hours of a quiet table, and that's the honest deal.
topic.moment: You sit in a café with a laptop for three hours on one drink, and nobody asks you to leave.

turn.believed: Café coffee is a scam for people who want to look premium.
turn.actually: Our cities have almost no public places to sit, so cafés sell space, and the coffee is the ticket.

topic.because: Small homes, crowded offices and few libraries mean a table with Wi-Fi is scarce. The café prices the space into the cup.
topic.payoff: The coffee is ₹350. The chair is the product.
topic.behaviour: People work, date and hold meetings in cafés for hours on one order.
topic.mechanism: Space is scarce, so it gets sold disguised as a drink.
topic.send_to: The friend who complains about café prices from the same café every weekend.
topic.why_now: Café chains keep opening across cities while rents climb.

score.why: The chair is the product, not the coffee. A fair-deal view of something people grumble about.

topic.villain: a city with no public places left to sit

The take's premise is wrong: The post's load-bearing premise — that cafés tolerate hours-on-one-order because 'a full room of laptops is the best signboard it has,' i.e. long-stay campers work as advertising that makes the low per-table revenue worthwhile. In the actual trade this is mostly backwards: laptop campers are widely treated as a revenue problem, not a marketing asset.. How it actually works: A café's economics run on table turnover and average ticket size, not on seats-as-advertising: the drink carries a 70–85% gross margin but net margins are only ~3–7%, so a four-top held for three hours on one $4–5 coffee earns roughly $1/hour and many operators actively fight it — cutting Wi-Fi, covering outlets, setting time limits, redesigning for fast turnover (one documented laptop ban tripled ticket size and lifted profit ~35%). When a café does let you linger, the real reasons are that rent/labour/lights are sunk fixed costs so the marginal cost of an already-seated customer is near zero, plus a busy room is mild social proof for walk-ins — not that your laptop is a billboard recruiting more laptops. So the consumer intuition 'you're renting the table, not buying the coffee' is roughly right, but the stated causal story for why the café welcomes it is wrong. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

ledger.text: Cafés tolerate customers staying for hours on one order because a room full of long-staying laptop users functions as a signboard that attracts more customers, making the long stay commercially worthwhile for the café despite low per-table revenue.
ledger.sentence: And the café isn't fighting your long stay. A full room of laptops is the best signboard it has.

ledger.text: Public libraries in many Indian towns have shut down, or such towns never had one.
ledger.sentence: The library shut years ago, if your town ever had one.

ledger.text: In Indian cities there are almost no free public spaces to sit for extended periods, since most quiet corners are privately owned by shops.
ledger.sentence: Then you step outside and look for a free chair. Every quiet corner belongs to someone's shop.

c2.correct: Both halves hold, but as a structural/rural-urban gap rather than a single news event: (1) many existing town/city libraries have shut branches or decayed — e.g. Mumbai's 125-year-old Mumbai Marathi Granthalaya has only 29 of its 44 branches open (21 active) due to funding and political problems, and libraries nationwide lost members during COVID-19 and never recovered; (2) most small towns and almost all villages never had one — 2011 census data shows only ~4,580 libraries existed in all of urban India (about one per 80,000 urban residents), and government library laws exist in only 19 states with implementation hampered by chronic underfunding (e.g. Bengaluru's BBMP owed ₹226+ crore in library cess as of 2019). A 2019 national government survey counted 46,746 public libraries total, up from 27,682 earlier, but even this growth is concentrated in a handful of states (Maharashtra, Kerala, Karnataka) leaving large swathes of small towns with no coverage.

sources.publisher: Raja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation, Ministry of Culture, Govt. of India
sources.quote: Qualitative and Quantitative Survey Of Public Libraries in India ... final survey report submitted in July 2019; India has a total of 46,746 public libraries across States and Union Territories

Of its 44 branches, only 29 are currently open, with just 21 actively operational ... Dwindling memberships, funds crunch and societal apathy are emerging as the primary reasons for many libraries closing down
According to the 2011 census, India has only 4,580 libraries in urban areas ... one urban library for over 80,000 people

In almost all states, the local departments of libraries point to lack of funding as the main impediment to offering services ... the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP), owes more than Rs 226 crore to the Department of Public Libraries as on 2019

c3.correct: Confirmed and still current as of the Nov 2026 go-live date: Indian cities have far less usable public open space than international norms (WHO recommends 9 sq m/person), and much of what exists is being converted into monetizable, privately-controlled space rather than free seating areas. Reported per-capita figures: Mumbai ~1.2–1.58 sq m, Chennai ~0.81 sq m, Patna ~2.43 sq m, national urban average ~2.7 sq m, versus London (31.7 sq m) and New York (26.4 sq m). Multiple 2025–2026 pieces describe cafes/malls effectively charging an 'entry fee' (e.g., a ₹300 coffee) to sit, because benches and parks generate no revenue and are deprioritized in planning.

sources.quote: Per capita open space in Indian cities currently stands at about 2.7 square meters, far below the World Health Organization's recommended minimum of 9 square meters.
Mumbai's city average hovers around 1.2 square metres per person ... The ₹300 cappuccino is not a beverage. It is the entry ticket required to buy the right to sit.

The privatisation of public spaces is not just a byproduct of urbanisation; in many cities, it's part of the plan ... What gets developed, malls, gated communities, and commercial parks with restricted access, shares one common trait: it is space that can be monetised.
areas where people engaged as citizens are gradually being replaced by spaces of consumption, dividing our cities even more and shrinking the realm of public discourse

mechanism.actual_mechanism: A café drink is priced at roughly 4–5x its ingredient cost: beans, milk and cup run only ~15–25% of the menu price, while the remaining ~75–85% covers labor, rent and overhead — i.e., the room, the air-con, the wifi and the seat. _ledger.text:
[cover] A coffee is the cheapest [rent] in your city
You're not buying the drink. Look around the table.
 

[slide 1] A coffee is the cheapest rent in your city.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's a Saturday. You've had the corner table for three hours. One cold coffee, finished an hour ago, the ice gone to water, a wet ring spreading on the wood.

[slide 3] You keep bracing for the waiter to clear your glass and give you that look.
Instead he tops up your water and walks off. You feel like you're getting away with something.

[slide 4] So run the list of places you could have sat for free today.
Your flat, bed two steps from the laptop. The office, dark and dead on a weekend. A park with no plug point. A library, if one still stands near you.
None of them hold you for three hours.

[slide 5] That's the honest deal, and it's a fair one. A small flat, a packed office, no bench that's free and shaded.
The city ran out of places to sit. Someone built one, put air-con and Wi-Fi inside, and a price on the door.

[slide 6] At hour four you order a second one. Not because you're thirsty. Because the table is worth paying for again, and you both know it.

[end card] Open this again the next time you nurse one coffee for three hours.
Send to the friend who complains about café prices from the same café every weekend.
